newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang to formally respond to talks offer-radio.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang to formally respond to talks offer-radio.

text.p: North Korea has proposed a meeting with U.S. and South Korean officials this month to give its formal response to a proposal for four-way peace talks, state radio reported on Saturday.
The Korea Broadcasting system said Seoul authorities had given a "favourable response" to the suggestion for a meeting.
It said the offer was made in a meeting between officials from the two Koreas and the United states in New York on Friday.
There was no indication of whether Pyongyang wanted the meeting to give a positive response or reject the offer or set further conditions for participation.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam and U.S. President Bill Clinton proposed the four-way talks, also including China, last April.
The talks are aimed at establishing a permanent peace to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean war.
State radio quoted an unnamed government source as saying the meeting would take place this month.
The Munwha Ilbo newspaper cited a South Korean Embassy official in the United States saying it would take place around April 22.
South Korean government officials were not immediately available for comment on the new reports.
In its first formal response to the U.S.-South Korean peace initiative, Pyongyang last month demanded substantial food aid as a condition for taking part in any peace talks.
Seoul and Washington rejected preconditions but said food aid could be discussed as part of the four-way talks.
South Korea pledged $6 million and the United States $10 million to a $41 million World Food Programme (WFP) appeal in aid for impoverished North Korea, which is on the brink of famine.

The WFP on Friday more than doubled the appeal to $95 million to feed 2.6 million babies and toddlers aged under six in the Stalinist state. Seoul and Washington have not announced whether they will boost their contribution.
